CHN.story:
China opened intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by parents in other countries, in 1992. About 160,000 children were sent abroad, most of them to the United States, which issued visas to 87,704 children adopted from China between 1994 and 2014. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought babies from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with families in China and abroad. In 2005, 23 officials were fired and three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years in prison. The New Yorker reported that the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking, and on 5 September 2024 China ended it.

Girls and women are also brought into China from neighbouring countries and sold as brides. Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States in Myanmar, many displaced by war, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to $13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the AP news agency that the investigation largely stopped because of pressure from officials worried about relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals.

In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports of online abuse from technology companies, received 9,406 reports for China, compared with 1,933,900 for India, because most American platforms are blocked there. The extent of online abuse of children in China is therefore not known, and the trade in brides from neighbouring countries continues.

CIV.story:
Girls are moved within and into Côte d'Ivoire for work and sex. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and other West African countries to Abidjan, promising school or training, and then keep them as domestic servants, where they are vulnerable to sexual exploitation. Ivorian women and girls are sold for sex, especially in Abidjan. Nigerian traffickers recruit women and girls with offers of jobs in shops and then exploit them in the gold-mining and cocoa regions, as part of networks that also move Nigerian girls to mines in Senegal, Mali and Burkina Faso.

How many children in Côte d'Ivoire are sexually exploited is not known, because no representative survey has been done in West and Central Africa.

UKR.story:
Between 2012 and 2015 the US-based group Disability Rights International investigated 33 Ukrainian orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities, and concluded that the orphanage system served traffickers as a way to recruit children. La Strada Ukraine, an anti-trafficking charity, told it that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that sexual exploitation in institutions usually began around age 13, often started by staff. A coordinator for IOM, the UN migration agency, said most documented trafficking cases began in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. Ukraine also sent 18,612 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and the United States issued visas to 10,544 children adopted from Ukraine from 1994 to 2014.

After Russia's full invasion in February 2022, a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped children. The war also put children left in Ukrainian institutions at risk. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report said children evacuated from at least 195 facilities were at high risk, that officials at several state institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running.

Children who remain in Ukraine's institutions are at risk from traffickers, and no official has been convicted of taking part.

VNM.story:
The United States issued 7,498 immigrant visas to children adopted from Hanoi between 1994 and 2014, with a peak of 828 in 2007. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi reported that the number of babies recorded as abandoned had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the United States when it expired that September. In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two provincial social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, for "abuse of power and authority". They were accused of asking poor families for their babies and falsifying papers to say the babies had been abandoned, and 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008.

The US State Department's 2025 report on trafficking says traffickers in border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriage, and that Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024. In Britain, 416 Vietnamese children were referred to the authorities as possible trafficking victims in 2024, many of them exploited on cannabis farms and in nail salons.

Vietnam limited adoption to the United States after the embassy's report of fraud, and officials were put on trial for selling babies for adoption. The 2025 figures show children from poor and minority families still being trafficked abroad, to China and Britain among other places.

RUS.story:
From the 1990s Russia sent large numbers of children from its orphanages to families abroad. The United States issued visas to 60,266 children adopted from Russia between 1994 and 2014, with the most, 5,865, in 2004.

In May 2000 Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help with Blue Orchid, a Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By March 2001 four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, and leads were passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, acted on 5,797 web addresses in Russia, 2 percent of its total.

After a criminal case was opened against him in St Petersburg in November 2013, the priest Gleb Grozovsky fled to Israel. He was detained and extradited to Russia, the legal process of sending a suspect back for trial, and in 2018 he was jailed for 14 years. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped Ukrainian children.

In the cases recorded here, offenders were caught when Russian and foreign police worked together or when a suspect who had fled abroad was sent back. No trial over the UN commission's finding that Russian forces raped children is recorded in the sources for this map.

GRL.story:
The sources gathered for this map hold no case of sexual abuse, exploitation, sale or trafficking of children in Greenland. The one Greenland record they contain concerns a removal of children by the Danish state in 1951, and it documents none of these, so it is not shown.

No figures on sexual abuse or trafficking of children in Greenland are included in the sources for this map, so how many children there are affected is not known.

GRC.story:
In its 2025 trafficking report, the US State Department said unaccompanied migrant children in Greece are vulnerable to sex trafficking, and that Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg there. In April 2025 the US Department of Justice announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of '764 Inferno', a subgroup of the online network 764, which extorted minors into producing abuse material and harming themselves. One was arrested in North Carolina and the other in Greece.

Unaccompanied children arriving in Greece remain at risk of sex trafficking. No inquiry into the sexual abuse of children in Greek institutions was found in the sources for this map.

DNK.story:
In 2011 the Godhavn Report examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other Danish state children's homes from 1945 to 1976. It found neglect and physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22 percent of Godhavn's boys had been given psychiatric drugs by a psychiatrist. No prosecutions followed, and Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in 2019.

Denmark has also received many children from abroad, including 9,297 from South Korea between 1965 and 2008. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that agencies there had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Denmark suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2016 after abuses there, and in 2024 the Danish International Adoption agency, the country's only intercountry adoption agency, said it was closing.

Danish police have led or joined several international investigations of online abuse, from the Bamse bulletin board in the early 1990s to Operation Cumberland in 2025, one of the first cases of AI-generated abuse material, in which 273 suspects were identified.

The children abused in the state homes have received an apology from the prime minister, and no one was prosecuted. With its only agency closing, Denmark's part in intercountry adoption is ending.

BLR.story:
Until 2003 a company in Minsk called Regpay Co. Ltd took paid memberships for about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it ran itself, and sold access to thousands of subscribers around the world. Subscribers paid by credit card, the payments passed through Latvian banks, and a Florida payment firm, Connections, helped hide where the money came from. Because the company was in Belarus, beyond the reach of US police, US agents used a ruse to draw its president, Yahor Zalatarou, and its marketing director to a hotel in Paris, where they were arrested in July 2003; the technical administrator was arrested in Spain and extradited. All three pleaded guilty in New Jersey, and in 2006 Zalatarou and the administrator were each sentenced to 25 years. The customer records led to the arrest of hundreds of subscribers in the US and other countries, in what the US government called Operation Falcon.

Regpay's managers were tried only after US agents drew them out of Belarus. The sources for this map record no other case of child abuse networks run from Belarus.

BGR.story:
In its 2025 trafficking report the US State Department cited a UN special rapporteur, an independent expert appointed by the UN, who found that sexual exploitation, including possible sex trafficking, was common among children in government-run institutions. The same report said traffickers exploit Bulgarian girls and women in Sofia, in resort and border towns and across Western Europe. It found corruption widespread in the police and the courts, and of 31 traffickers convicted, only eight were sent to prison.

Bulgaria sent 5,067 children abroad for adoption between 2003 and 2022, and its adoptions remain open.

Bulgaria now hosts more of the online abuse material found by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes such material, than any other country. In 2025 the foundation acted on 87,959 web addresses in Bulgaria, 28 percent of its total, up from 9 percent in 2024, and said most of them belonged to a few particular sites. Bulgarian cybercrime police have also taken servers down, as in 2017–18, when they removed the servers of a subscription site showing the abuse of boys in Thailand.

Children in Bulgarian state institutions remain at risk of sexual exploitation, and most convicted traffickers do not go to prison. In 2025 a few sites hosted in Bulgaria accounted for more than a quarter of the abuse material the foundation found.

CHE.story:
Swiss federal and cantonal authorities, the national and regional governments, detained people without any court order. An independent expert commission reported in 2019 that more than 60,000 people had been held in about 650 institutions, mainly between 1930 and 1981, and that many were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. Among them were the Verdingkinder, children placed with farmers as unpaid labourers. The government had apologised in 2010, and a 2016 law gave each victim of these measures a payment of CHF 25,000.

Switzerland also received children for adoption from abroad, including 1,111 from South Korea between 1968 and 1997 and others from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet. Swiss authorities realised early that the children were often wrongly described as orphans and that some adoptions were linked to organised child trafficking, yet they decided cases on incomplete or false documents. After parliament commissioned a study in 2018, the Federal Council, Switzerland's government, acknowledged these failures in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 it recommended banning intercountry adoption altogether.

In 2023 historians at the University of Zurich, working for the Catholic bishops and religious orders, documented 921 victims of abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the 1950s; 74 percent of the documents concerned abuse of minors. They described their count as the tip of the iceberg.

Switzerland has examined and apologised for detentions and forced placements carried out by its own authorities, and has paid victims of these measures. The researchers' count of victims in the Catholic Church is a minimum, and the full number is not known.

FRA.story:
Between 1968 and 2008 France took in 11,165 children from South Korea for adoption, among others from abroad. In March 2024 a government assessment acknowledged that the authorities had long known of "illicit practices of a systemic nature" in intercountry adoption and had been late to act.

In 2018 the Catholic bishops set up an independent commission chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé. Its 2021 report used a population survey to estimate that about 216,000 people had been abused as minors by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, or about 330,000 if lay people working for the Church were included.

In 2004 the US FBI traced downloads of abuse images to the surgeon Joël Le Scouarnec, and in 2005 a French court gave him a four-month suspended sentence. Prosecutors did not tell the medical authorities, a warning to the health ministry in 2007 led to no action, and in 2008 a hospital hired him knowing of the conviction. He went on abusing patients until 2014. In 2025 he admitted abusing 299 victims, many of them under anaesthesia, and was sentenced to 20 years.

In April 2025 a parliamentary inquiry estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services are victims of prostitution. Teenagers in care are often housed in hotels with little supervision.

France has estimated the scale of abuse in the Church through a national survey and has given victims more time to bring a case. By the inquiry's estimate, about 15,000 children in the state's own care are being sold for sex now.

GHA.story:
Among the Ewe people of Ghana, some traditional shrines practise trokosi. A shrine takes a girl, usually a young virgin, to atone for a wrong a relative is said to have committed. She serves the priest without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as part of her duty, which defenders of the practice deny. In 1998 Ghana amended its Criminal Code to make ritual or customary servitude a crime, with a minimum sentence of three years. The practice continued, and no prosecutions are recorded.

Children are also sold into work. On Lake Volta, traffickers put children as young as four to work in fishing and control them with violence and little food. In 2023 International Justice Mission, a charity, surveyed 1,286 children in three fishing districts and estimated that 37.7 percent were likely to have been trafficked. The US State Department said in 2025 that girls in the fishing trade are at risk of sexual exploitation, and that observers reported forced child labour on the lake had decreased.

Some Ghanaian boys were taken further away. In 2019 police in Kaduna, in northern Nigeria, raided a building presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 boys and men, many of them in chains. Some had been brought from Ghana, Burkina Faso and Mali, and local media reported that captives had been sexually abused.

No representative survey of online sexual exploitation of children has been carried out in West and Central Africa, so its extent in Ghana is not known. Children are still put to work on Lake Volta, and trokosi continued after it was made a crime.

ISR.story:
In March 2008 the Adass Israel School, an ultra-Orthodox school in Melbourne, paid for its headmistress, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of allegations that she had abused pupils. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences. Her lawyers in Israel sought more than 70 hearings and appeals, and in 2019 she was found to have faked mental illness. The deputy health minister, Yaakov Litzman, had pressured ministry staff to change psychiatric evaluations so that she would appear unfit for extradition, the legal process of sending a suspect to another country for trial. Leifer was extradited in 2021 and convicted in Melbourne in 2023 of 18 charges including rape. Litzman admitted breach of trust in a plea deal, resigned from the Knesset, Israel's parliament, and received eight months' probation.

In June 2024 a UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israeli security forces had subjected Palestinians to sexual violence during arrests and in detention, that men and boys were targeted in particular ways, and that this amounted to gender persecution as a crime against humanity. It also found that sexual violence was committed in the attacks of 7 October 2023, when 36 children were among 252 people taken hostage.

Leifer was convicted in Australia in 2023 after years of hearings in Israel, and the minister who obstructed her extradition received probation.
